title: Chapter 8: Carried Out by the Elbow
content: Ruthie Pyle keeps the ledger under the register, on a shelf built for phone books, and she has it open on the counter before Wren's coffee is poured. It is a school notebook with a black cover, the same kind she has bought every September since 1989, one line to a customer, dated at the front.

The Bend Diner at twenty to seven: six men at the counter, two booths full, the grill going, the window fogged in one corner where the coffee machine steams. Wren sits at the third stool, which is the one with the wobble, and Ruthie sets the cup down and stands over her with her arms folded.
"Don't touch it," Ruthie says. "I'll turn the pages. You've got river on your hands."
"I washed my hands."
"You've got river on your hands anyway."
She turns the notebook around with two fingers, the way a dealer turns a card.
"Read the fourteenth," Ruthie says.
Wren reads.
22 Sept. D. Hollister: she ruined the Revival. My sister's bridge club says the same. E. Pyle: she said a true thing in a rude room.
"Who is E. Pyle?"
"Me." Ruthie wipes the counter. "I write what's said. I don't write what's true. That's the difference between a ledger and a Bible."
"Then why did you write yours?"
"Because I was there, and I've got a column, and I'm sixty-six years old." She takes the pot back to the machine. "It's the only entry like it. Don't get comfortable."

Wren turns the page with the back of her spoon. The twenty-second runs to nine lines. M. Cady: my husband has a bad heart, he doesn't need a scene. T. Boyle: that's the last time I vote for a bond. Anonymous, left no name but left a dollar: the ferry is a coffin with a schedule.
"That last one's not bad," Wren says.
"It's not wrong, either." Ruthie comes back. "You want eggs?"
"No."
"You'll eat eggs." She writes the ticket. "You're down nine pounds. I can see it in your neck."

The door opens and the room does a thing Wren has never felt in this diner in her life. It does not go silent. It goes careful. Two men at the counter turn their shoulders a few degrees away from her, and the booth by the window stops talking and starts listening, and a woman in a blue cardigan picks up her purse and sets it on her lap.
Ruthie watches all of it and writes nothing, and that is its own entry.
The eggs come. Wren eats four bites.

Mars is in the back booth with a file folder and a cup of coffee gone cold, and she has been there long enough that Ruthie has stopped refilling it. Mars Okonjo has three pens in her bag and a county ID on a lanyard she takes off before she sits down anywhere, and she moves the folder to the wall side of the table when Wren sits.
"Do you want the good news," Mars says, "or the thing I came here to say?"
"Say the thing."

"Ottoline Reeve makes one phone call a year." Mars keeps her voice low and pleasant, a woman discussing a cousin. "One. Last year it was to the state liquor board about the Pines, because the Pines put a patio in without a permit and a councilman's nephew got a DUI off that patio. The Pines lost its license in eleven days. Eleven. They're serving sandwiches now out of a window."
"I don't have a license."

"You have a boat," Mars says. "You have a house on a flood easement. You have a grandfather with no death certificate, which means the estate is open, which means the county can look at the easement, and the county answers to her on water matters." She turns the cup a quarter turn. "She's already made this year's call. I heard the clerk say the word Aubrey on the phone Monday and then she closed her door."
Wren puts her fork down.
"Then she's ahead of schedule."
"That's not funny."
"It wasn't a joke."
Mars rubs her eyes. She has a way of being frightened that looks like being tired, and Wren has known her for eleven years and can tell the difference.

"Nine years I've worked in that basement," Mars says. "You know what I've learned? Nobody gets ended in one go. They get ended in paper. A letter that goes to the wrong address. A form that needs a signature from a man who retired. You'll still be here. You'll just be here with nothing."
"Then I'll be here."
Mars looks at her for a long moment and then opens the folder, and it is empty, and she closes it again.
"Wednesday," she says. "After six. I'm not saying anything else in a diner."
She takes her folder and her three pens and her cold coffee and leaves, and the bell over the door does its cheerful two notes, and the booth by the window watches her go.
Wren finishes the eggs because Ruthie is watching.
Then she takes her cup to the register and stands there until Ruthie looks up.
"Write this down."
"I don't take dictation."
"You take testimony." Wren puts the cup on the rubber mat. "You've got a column and I've got a sentence."
Ruthie's mouth does something complicated behind her glasses. She pulls the ledger around, uncaps the pen, and holds it over the page, and does not write.
"Say it slow."
"W. Aubrey." Wren watches the pen. "The ferry ran nine today. Nobody drowned."
The pen stops. Ruthie looks up.
"That's not testimony. That's a claim."
"It's a true thing," Wren says, "in a room that's been rude to me all morning."

Ruthie writes it. She writes it slowly, and then she puts the date at the front of the line, 23 Sept., and rules a small line under it with the edge of the pen, which she does not do for anybody else.
"Nine," Ruthie says. "That's down from forty on a Wednesday in June."
"I know what it's down from."
"All right." Ruthie closes the ledger and puts it under the register. "Eat something at noon. I'll know if you don't."

At the register, Ruthie has the county paper taped up beside the lottery sign. Page one, above the fold: a photograph of a woman with her back to the camera, arm up, microphone in her fist, the tent lights blown out white behind her. The caption is four lines. The headline is one.
FERRYMAN'S GRANDDAUGHTER SPEAKS.
Wren reads her own name in print for the first time. It looks like somebody else's.
"Two people bought the paper and asked me if I knew you," Ruthie says. "One of them was nice about it."

The landing at one o'clock is hot and the cable is singing in the sun, a low note you feel in your teeth. Ade Kessler is on the east deck with the grease gun, and he does not look up when she comes down the ramp.
"Cable's fine," he says.
"I didn't ask."
"You were going to." He pumps the gun twice and sets it in the toolbox. "I checked it twice. Once at six, once at eight. Sheave's dry on the north side, so I packed it."
"Thank you."
"Don't."
He is a big man who has learned to take up less room than he needs, and he does it now, moving to the far end of the deck so she can have the winch.

The two o'clock run carries four. The three o'clock carries one, a man from the feed store who sits in the middle of the bench with his hands on his knees and says, at the far bank, "I'm sorry about your grandfather," and then, "My wife was at that thing Saturday," and gets off before she can answer.

The four o'clock carries nobody, which has not happened on a Wednesday in September in Wren's memory. There is a man on the east bank with a grocery sack, waiting, and when she brings the boat in he does not get on.
"I'll take the long way," he says.
The long way is eleven miles and one bridge.
"That's four gallons of gas," Wren says, "and the ferry's two dollars."
"I know what the ferry costs." He shifts the sack to his other arm. "I was at the Revival. My daughter sang in the choir that opened it. She's eleven."
Wren holds the boat against the piling with one hand. The water is going past at a walking pace, brown and easy, and behind the man the road is empty all the way to Mill Street.
"Then she should see the river working," Wren says. "Bring her down Saturday. I'll take her across for free and she can put her hand on the cable."
The man looks at her for a while.
"That's not what I meant," he says, and walks up the ramp.
She makes the crossing anyway. It is in the schedule and the schedule is the only thing she has left that the Authority has not taken.
At five, Ade says, "You want me to say something to them?"
"To who?"
"To the ones who won't ride." He has his cap off and is turning it in his hands. "I could say something."
"No."
"All right."
He puts the cap back on and goes to check the cable a third time, and she stands at the winch and understands, in a way that has no words attached to it, that he is not going to leave.

The last run is at seven forty. The water is going gold and the gate lights come on upstream, three red dots, and she lands the boat and ties off and does the log, name and date, nine names for the day, and the number looks like an accusation.
Then she goes down to the take-up drum with a flashlight, because the wheel has been loud all afternoon, a scrape on the half turn.

The housing is a steel box the size of a loaf of bread, bolted to the frame where the cable comes off the drum and enters the sheave. It holds grease and it holds the cable straight and it is not complicated. Wren puts the light on it and stops.
There is a line across the top of it, bright and clean, and when she puts her thumb on it the metal rocks.

She wipes the grease away with two fingers. The cut goes down through the wall of the housing and three quarters of the way through the flange, and the blade has left a curl of steel, and the curl is still there, and there are filings in the grease like black sand.
She stands up. The river is going dark and the far bank is a line of trees and the road light at Mill Street comes on with a click she can hear because there is nothing else.

She walks the frame with the light. The padlock on the gate is locked. The bolt heads on the housing are untouched, no wrench marks, nothing stripped. There is a clean place in the gravel by the drum where a foot went in and came out again, and the print is a work boot, size ten or eleven, and it points at the water.
Wren stands over the print for a long time with the flashlight pointed down.
The cut is on the river side. It faces the water, not the road, not the yard, not the gate where the cars come through.
Whoever did it came by boat.
highlight: Ruthie's ledger fills against her, and somebody saws through the ferry cable housing from the water side.
